evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-stricken Catholic father hunts the family that murdered his wife and children, while his cop sister and a conflicted Risaldi son race to stop him before vengeance becomes his only faith.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional engine is immediate: murdered family, revenge, guilt, and a faith-based moral frame. The audience is narrower than a broad four-quadrant crime thriller because of the heavy Catholic specificity and sustained tragedy, but the hook is clear and commercially legible.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the opening massacre and then sharpens into a revenge-versus-redemption chase. Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor are all easy to track as the story pivots from aftermath to confrontation.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob’s wounded righteousness, Jodie’s professional and personal conflict, and Ethan’s moral fracture give the script real acting terrain. Victor is a strong antagonist, but several Risaldi brothers function more as pressure points than fully individualized characters.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Catholic confession structure, choir/music motifs, and repeated spiritual language give the piece a distinct identity. The underlying revenge-crime spine is familiar, but the script commits to its religious register in a way that feels specific.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps moving through raids, funerals, interrogations, and converging confrontations, with a clear escalation toward the mansion finale. Some middle passages lean on dialogue-heavy moral debate, but the forward drive remains intact.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a devout man becoming an executioner is instantly understandable and thematically sticky. What keeps it from the highest band is that the revenge framework itself is familiar, even though the faith lens gives it a fresh emotional angle.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a textured world of church life, police bureaucracy, family hierarchy, and criminal ritual. The Risaldi mansion, adoration chapel, docks, club, and confessional all feel story-generating rather than generic.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually committed: operatic violence, devotional language, grief, and moral pleading all sit in the same frame. The repeated hymns, confessions, and public prayer scenes give the script a recognizable spiritual-crime identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real undercurrents around guilt, inherited violence, masculinity, and the difference between justice and vengeance. The script signals more interior life than it can fully explore in a single feature, especially through Ethan, Victor, and Father Michael.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jacob/Jodie, Jacob/Ethan, Ethan/Victor, and Victor/Alicia all generate tension and reversals. It is not a true ensemble machine, but the family web is strong enough that multiple pairings can carry scenes.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, white, Catholic, working-class father and older brother.
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is a devastated family man whose grief curdles into purpose. He starts as the emotionally hollow survivor of a massacre, then becomes a man willing to cross every line in the name of justice, even as his faith keeps offering him a way back.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Joel Edgerton in The Gift: a contained, grief-saturated lead who has to play quiet collapse, sudden violence, and moral self-interrogation in the same role.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, white, police officer, Jacob’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is the cop who cannot separate duty from family. She is professionally hard-edged but emotionally exposed, and the script keeps forcing her to choose between the law, her brother, and the truth she can barely survive hearing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk or Amy Adams in Sharp Objects so much traction: a controlled, high-intensity emotional role where restraint is the performance.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, white, morally conflicted member of the Risaldi family.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the family’s conscience and its liability. He is intelligent, frightened, and desperate to believe in absolution, which makes him both the most humane Risaldi and the one most likely to betray them.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally split, spiritually searching role that let Adam Driver in Silence or Paul Dano in Prisoners play intelligence, shame, and vulnerability without losing tension.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 60s, white, patriarch of the Risaldi family.
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the script’s cold engine of authority: composed, humiliating, and terrifyingly certain that cruelty is governance. He treats his sons as instruments, his wife as property, and meaning itself as something he alone gets to define.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime Brian Cox in Succession or Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men territory: a dominant, scene-commanding patriarch role that lets an actor weaponize stillness, contempt, and control.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, violent, unstable Risaldi son.
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s most volatile predator, but the script also lets him register as a broken son desperate for approval. He is theatrical, sadistic, and deeply wounded, which makes him dangerous and oddly tragic at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, high-wire villain role that gave Jack O’Connell in Starred Up or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom a chance to be terrifying and pitiable in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, younger Risaldi brother.
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the family member who still wants to believe obedience can protect him. He is less monstrous than the others, which makes his fear and eventual collapse more painful than simple villainy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting-actor material in the vein of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire: a role built on suppressed panic and sudden moral fracture.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, physically imposing enforcer.
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument, a man who does the worst things with the least visible language. He is not the most articulate Risaldi, but he is one of the most frightening because he acts without hesitation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of physically grounded menace role that lets an actor work in the lane of Tom Hardy in Bronson or Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire: minimal speech, maximum threat.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, white, Victor’s wife, former stripper.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is trapped inside the family’s hierarchy but never fully erased by it. The script gives her humiliation, fear, and a late-stage moral clarity that makes her more than a victimized accessory to Victor’s rule.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised, lived-in role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Laura Linney in Ozark a chance to play fear, dignity, and resignation with precision.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the script’s spiritual counterweight: warm, funny, and doctrinally firm without becoming abstract. He gives the story its language of grace, but he also knows grace does not stop bloodshed on its own.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Mark Rylance did in Bridge of Spies or Brendan Gleeson in Calvary: authority through compassion, with real thematic weight.

lead_characters.name: Captain Ricks
lead_characters.hook: Ricks is the weary institutional face of the case, trying to manage optics, evidence, and grief without ever fully controlling any of them. He is not the moral center, but he gives the procedural world credibility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor terrain in the vein of Jeffrey Wright in The Batman or Shea Whigham in any number of crime dramas: a grounded authority role with pressure and fatigue baked in.

lead_characters.name: Chief Pitts
lead_characters.hook: Pitts is the more public-facing institutional voice, trying to sound humane while still protecting the machine. He has enough conscience to apologize, but not enough power to fix what the city has already become.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that gives an actor a chance to play compromised decency, like John Carroll Lynch in Zodiac or Clark Gregg in The West Wing.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Owens
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Owens is a brief but important stabilizing presence, the person who can see Jacob’s self-destruction before he can. She functions as a humane professional counterpoint to the script’s more punitive voices.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, scene-specific role with the kind of emotional authority that lets an actor make a small part feel essential, like Jennifer Ehle in Zero Dark Thirty.

lead_characters.name: Xavier Winters
lead_characters.hook: Xavier is the decent outsider who has built a life around someone else’s trauma. He is not the engine of the story, but he gives Lucy’s testimony a domestic frame and a real-world cost.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a grounded supporting role in the lane of a restrained indie husband part, the kind that lets an actor play patience, concern, and helplessness without overplaying.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Winters
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 30s, white, survivor and mother.
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is one of the script’s most painful witnesses: composed on the surface, shattered underneath, and finally willing to name what happened to her. Her testimony widens the story from family revenge into a broader pattern of abuse and power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of devastating testimony role that gave Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman a chance to turn pain into force.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the script’s last remaining innocence inside the Risaldi house. He is quiet, observant, and terrifyingly vulnerable, which makes him the emotional future the story is trying to save.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong child role with real emotional stakes, the kind that can anchor a late-film rescue beat and give a young actor a memorable, non-sentimental turn.

multiple male roles in the 20s-60s range
several roles require intense intimidation or grief performance

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical; limited atmospheric work for snow, smoke, fire, and a few stylized transitions/montage moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, blood effects, fire damage, practical body effects, and a few fight beats in the alley and club.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a prestige crime thriller with awards-adjacent dramatic weight.

budget.note: The script is contemporary and mostly interior-driven, but the club fire, docks raid, snow coverage, blood effects, and multiple company moves will keep it above a lean contained-thriller footprint.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor all need actors who can carry grief, menace, and moral argument without flattening into genre types. The child role for Marcus and the younger Risaldi brothers add sensitivity to the search.

development.note: The faith-versus-vengeance framework is distinctive, but the script leans heavily on long dialogue confrontations and repeated moral articulation, so the buyer conversation will focus on whether the emotional engine stays as sharp as the premise.

comp_set.title: Manchester by the Sea
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-damaged lead carrying unbearable family loss, with the emotional weight living in silence, guilt, and self-punishment.

comp_set.title: Calvary
comp_set.why_it_comps: Catholic moral inquiry colliding with violence and community rot, with a priestly spiritual frame that never becomes decorative.

comp_set.title: Prisoners
comp_set.why_it_comps: A desperate father, a morally compromised investigation, and a revenge engine that keeps tightening around the family unit.

comp_set.title: A History of Violence
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script shares the idea of a family man forced into violent reckoning while the past keeps reasserting itself.

comp_set.title: Wind River
comp_set.why_it_comps: Bleak crime-thriller momentum, winter atmosphere, and a justice story shaped by grief and institutional failure.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to prestige crime dramas with moral weight, especially viewers drawn to grief, faith, and revenge stories with strong acting showcases.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but with strong female appeal through Jodie and the family-loss angle; educated streaming/theatrical specialty audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary, interior-heavy crime drama with a handful of night exteriors, practical violence, and a limited number of major set pieces.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult, actor-forward crime drama with a spiritual spine. The church material, family tragedy, and contained production footprint make it attractive to buyers looking for elevated genre with awards-capable performances.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the Risaldi family is vivid, but the story resolves the central conflict and does not present a clean sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a clear thematic moat: revenge is filtered through confession, grace, and sin rather than generic crime-movie catharsis. That gives buyers a sharper marketing angle and gives actors a reason to lean into the material as more than a standard vengeance piece.
strengths.evidence: The confession booth scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and Jacob’s repeated Act of Contrition structure the ending and the emotional vocabulary of the film.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a real showcase role
strengths.what_it_means: A lead like this can attract a serious actor looking to reset perception with a wounded, morally compromised father. The role offers grief, rage, restraint, and a final collapse into violence and remorse.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy breakdown, the alley fight with Tyler, the mansion confrontation, and the final confession all ask for different registers from the same performer.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Risaldi patriarch is a strong villain package
strengths.what_it_means: Victor gives the project a memorable antagonist who can anchor trailers, scene-steal, and elevate the whole package. A commanding older actor can make the film feel bigger than its budget by sheer presence.
strengths.evidence: Victor humiliates his sons, controls the room through silence, and turns family members into instruments of punishment in the ballroom scenes.

strengths.what_it_means: The story has enough locations and institutions to feel expansive without becoming expensive. That makes it easier to package as a prestige indie rather than a sprawling crime epic.
strengths.evidence: Church, police station, mansion, docks, club, apartment, graveyard, and confession booth all recur as distinct story spaces.

strengths.what_it_means: Jacob, Jodie, and Ethan create a three-way moral pressure system that keeps the climax from being a simple shootout. That kind of relational tension is attractive to buyers because it gives the ending emotional consequence beyond body count.
strengths.evidence: The final ballroom sequence forces Jacob’s vengeance, Jodie’s duty, and Ethan’s plea for meaning into the same room.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime thriller with a built-in emotional and spiritual hook: a Catholic father’s revenge story that can be sold as acting material first and genre second. The production footprint stays in indie range while the villain, the confession structure, and the family tragedy give it the kind of packaging clarity buyers can understand fast.

items.area: The opening massacre is extremely front-loaded
items.detail: The first pages deliver a brutal family slaughter before the audience has fully settled into the family dynamic, which makes the script’s emotional buy-in depend on immediate trust in the premise. That is effective for shock and urgency, but it also narrows the room for a slower emotional ramp.

items.area: The middle leans on long moral dialogue
items.detail: Several key stretches, especially the chapel, therapy, and confrontation scenes, are built on characters explaining grief, justice, and sin rather than forcing those ideas through action. That gives the film its identity, but it also creates a buyer conversation about whether the script is more sermon than propulsion in places.

Martin, Tyler, Edward, and Frankie each have a distinct function in the plot, but only Victor and Martin feel fully individualized on the page. For a crime family story, that means some of the antagonistic pressure reads as interchangeable rather than cumulatively specific.

items.area: The music clearance list is real
items.detail: The script names multiple songs and hymns, including Come Back, O Holy Night, 500 Miles, Clair de Lune, Good Looking, and L’Amour Toujours. That is manageable, but it is not invisible, and the music budget/clearance conversation will be part of any greenlight discussion.

Jay’s murder, the child endangerment, and the repeated family executions push the material into very dark territory. That is part of the script’s power, but it also narrows the buyer pool to platforms and distributors comfortable with sustained trauma and explicit brutality.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is not concept clarity; it’s how often the drama pauses to articulate its moral thesis in dialogue. Add a very real music-clearance list and a punishing level of onscreen violence, and the project becomes a strong but selective buy rather than a broad one.
